--- title: "Lab 5: Bikeshare SpaceTime Prediction" subtitle: "Rebalancing Indego in Philadelphia" author: "Wesley Nay" date: today format: html: code-fold: show code-tools: true toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-location: left theme: cosmo embed-resources: true editor: visual execute: warning: false message: false --- # INTRODUCTION ## The Rebalancing Challenge in Philadelphia Philadelphia's Indego bike share system faces the same operational challenge as every bike share system: **rebalancing bikes to meet anticipated demand**. In this report, I adapt the in-class Q1 2025 exercise to **Q3 2025** because I am interested in a seasonal comparison between winter and summer. Using station-hour panel data, weather data, census tract characteristics, and lagged demand measures, I build and compare several predictive models for bike share demand. I then examine where the model performs well, where it struggles, and whether prediction errors have operational or equity implications. ## Research Goals This analysis addresses four main questions: 1. How do bike share demand patterns in **Q3 2025** differ from the in-class **Q1 2025** example? 2. Which model features improve predictive accuracy the most? 3. Where are prediction errors concentrated across space, time, and neighborhood context? 4. Can targeted feature engineering improve model performance in a meaningful way? # SET UP ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(lubridate) library(sf) library(tigris) library(tidycensus) library(riem) # For Philadelphia weather from ASOS stations library(viridis) # color scales for visualization library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(patchwork) library(scales) library(here) options(scipen = 999) # Get rid of scientific notation to make it look tidier ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plotTheme <- theme_minimal() + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10), plot.caption = element_text(size = 8), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, angle = 45, hjust = 1), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10), axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"), panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#D0D0D0", linewidth = 0.2), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), legend.position = "right" ) mapTheme <- theme_void() + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10), plot.caption = element_text(size = 8), legend.position = "right", plot.margin = margin(1, 1, 1, 1, "cm"), legend.key.height = unit(1, "cm"), legend.key.width = unit(0.2, "cm") ) palette5 <- c("#eff3ff", "#bdd7e7", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} census_api_key(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")) ``` ::: # IMPORT AND PREP DATA ## Load Indego Trip Data (Q3 2025) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Read Q3 2025 data indego <- read.csv("data/indego-trips-2025-q3.csv") # Quick look at the data glimpse(indego) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 465,464 Columns: 15 $ trip_id 1203073573, 1203073759, 1203073753, 1203073877, 12… $ duration 10, 19, 16, 19, 2, 6, 20, 4, 52, 3, 31, 9, 10, 9, … $ start_time "7/1/2025 0:06", "7/1/2025 0:11", "7/1/2025 0:13",… $ end_time "7/1/2025 0:16", "7/1/2025 0:30", "7/1/2025 0:29",… $ start_station 3163, 3304, 3394, 3207, 3061, 3320, 3201, 3078, 32… $ start_lat 39.94974, 39.94234, 39.92400, 39.95441, 39.95425, … $ start_lon -75.18097, -75.15399, -75.16959, -75.19200, -75.17… $ end_station 3374, 3315, 3394, 3368, 3156, 3320, 3196, 3235, 32… $ end_lat 39.97280, 39.94235, 39.92400, 39.97647, 39.95381, … $ end_lon -75.17971, -75.21138, -75.16959, -75.17362, -75.17… $ bike_id "31674", "29473", "27889", "31825", "25400", "3172… $ plan_duration 30, 1, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30,… $ trip_route_category "One Way", "One Way", "Round Trip", "One Way", "On… $ passholder_type "Indego30", "Walk-up", "Indego30", "Indego30", "In… $ bike_type "electric", "electric", "electric", "electric", "e… ``` ::: ::: After a quick examination of the data, I see that the geography provided is in latitude and longitude. This suggests that the coordinate system is probably in WGS84, which is a standard lat-long coordinate system for the entire world. Before conducting spatial analysis, I will have to project these coordinates into an appropriate CRS for Philadelphia. The date and time structure of the data are currently stored as M/D/YY hour:minute (e.g., "7/1/2025 0:16"). These are character strings. This type of date and time structure might be difficult to work with later in the analysis, so I will have to adjust it into a proper datetime format using lubridate. Once parsed, I can create useful time variables for building the panel dataset that is necessary to work with bikeshare data like this. ## Examine the Data Structure ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The earliest trip was on July 1st at 6:00am and the latest trip was on September 30th at 11:58pm. In comparison to Q1 (January - March), Q3 (July - September) had much higher ridership. There were only 201,588 total trips in Q1. This is reasonable difference because Philadelphia experiences cold weather in the winter months of Q1, so people are less likely to want to ride bikes. Q3 is in the summer months, so the warmer weather can explain the higher total ridership. Additionally, it is probabaly more likely for tourists to visit Philadelphia in Q3 than in Q1, and tourism may also contribute to the higher ridership in Q3. ## Create Time Bins Next, I need need to aggregate trips into hourly intervals for my panel data structure. I will use the lubridate library for the date/time data extraction. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} indego <- indego %>% mutate( start_datetime = mdy_hm(start_time), end_datetime = mdy_hm(end_time), interval60 = floor_date(start_datetime, unit = "hour"), week = week(interval60), month = month(interval60, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE), dotw = wday(interval60, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE), hour = hour(interval60), date = as.Date(interval60), weekend = ifelse(dotw %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), 1, 0), rush_hour = ifelse(hour %in% c(7, 8, 9, 16, 17, 18), 1, 0) ) ``` ::: The interval60 variable is the backbone of the panel structure. It rounds each trip down to the beginning of the hour, making it possible to aggregate all trips that started within the same hour at the same station. This is what allows the analysis to move from individual trips to station-level hourly demand. # EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS ## Trips Over Time ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Daily trip counts daily_trips <- indego %>% group_by(date) %>% summarize(trips = n(), .groups = "drop") ggplot(daily_trips, aes(x = date, y = trips)) + geom_line(color = "#3182bd", linewidth = 1) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") + labs( title = "Indego Daily Ridership - Q3 2025", subtitle = "Summer to early fall demand patterns in Philadelphia", x = "Date", y = "Daily Trips", caption = "Source: Indego bike share" ) + plotTheme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/trips_over_time-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Ridership generally increases from the start of Q3 (July) through the end of September, but the slope is not gradual rather than steep. Ridership each month fluctuates, likely with increases during weekends. Weather may impact ridership as well during these summer months. There is one very steep dip September, which may be attributable to weather or some other limiting event. The fluctuations in ridership in Q3 are similar to what we saw in Q1, which likely reflects rider habits between weekdays and weekends. ## Holiday Checks ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} holiday_comparison <- tibble( date = as.Date(c("2025-07-04", "2025-09-01")), holiday = c("Independence Day", "Labor Day") ) %>% left_join(daily_trips, by = "date") %>% mutate( comparison_group = c("Typical Friday", "Typical Monday"), comparison_avg = c( indego %>% filter(dotw == "Fri", date != as.Date("2025-07-04")) %>% group_by(date) %>% summarize(trips = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% summarize(avg_trips = mean(trips)) %>% pull(avg_trips), indego %>% filter(dotw == "Mon", date != as.Date("2025-09-01")) %>% group_by(date) %>% summarize(trips = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% summarize(avg_trips = mean(trips)) %>% pull(avg_trips) ), difference = trips - comparison_avg ) kable( holiday_comparison %>% mutate( trips = comma(round(trips)), comparison_avg = comma(round(comparison_avg)), difference = round(difference, 0) ), caption = "Holiday Ridership Compared to Typical Same-Day Ridership" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

I thought that holidays might cause a spike in ridership, but the data did not reflect that. Both of these holidays had *lower* ridership than the average respective weekdays, as shown in the table printed above. This finding suggests that these summer holidays did not spike demand in Q3 as I initially expected. ## Hourly Patterns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Average trips by hour and day type hourly_patterns <- indego %>% group_by(hour, weekend) %>% summarize(avg_trips = n() / n_distinct(date), .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(day_type = ifelse(weekend == 1, "Weekend", "Weekday")) ggplot(hourly_patterns, aes(x = hour, y = avg_trips, color = day_type)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + scale_color_manual(values = c("Weekday" = "#08519c", "Weekend" = "#6baed6")) + labs( title = "Average Hourly Ridership Patterns", subtitle = "Comparing weekday and weekend demand in Q3 2025", x = "Hour of Day", y = "Average Trips per Hour", color = "Day Type" ) + plotTheme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/hourly_patterns-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: As seen above in the plot, weekdays actually have *higher* peaks than weekends in Q3. Ridership on weekdays peak in the morning around 8-9am and peak even higher in the evening around 5-6pm. This suggests that during the warm months of Q3, people are opting for Indego bikes as their form of commute to and from work. Unlike weekdays, the weekends do not have sharp peaks in Q3. Instead, ridership is more spread out throughout the day, gradually increasing from the late morning and peaking in the afternoon around 12-5pm. This suggests that ridership on the weekends may be more leisurely as people ride during peak sunny hours. While weekdays show a strong commuting pattern and weekends suggest leisurely rides, ridership for both weekdays and weekends taper off after about 6pm. ## Top Stations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Most popular origin stations top_stations <- indego %>% count(start_station, start_lat, start_lon, name = "trips") %>% arrange(desc(trips)) %>% slice_head(n = 20) kable( top_stations, caption = "Top 20 Indego Stations by Trip Origins", format.args = list(big.mark = ",") ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

This creates an issue for our analysis, since these stations cannot be linked to neighborhood-level demographic data. ## Dealing with missing data There are a few ways we can deal with these non-residential bike-share stations. In this analysis, I will remove them to keep things simple and to focus only on stations in residential neighborhoods. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Identify which stations to keep valid_stations <- stations_census %>% filter(!is.na(Med_Inc)) %>% pull(start_station) # Filter trip data to valid stations only indego_census <- indego %>% filter(start_station %in% valid_stations) %>% left_join( stations_census %>% select(start_station, Med_Inc, Percent_Taking_Transit, Percent_White, Total_Pop), by = "start_station" ) ``` ::: ## Get Weather Data Weather significantly affects bike share demand! Let's get hourly weather for Philadelphia. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Get weather from Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL) weather_data <- riem_measures( station = "PHL", date_start = "2025-07-01", date_end = "2025-09-30" ) weather_processed <- weather_data %>% mutate( interval60 = floor_date(valid, unit = "hour"), Temperature = tmpf, Precipitation = ifelse(is.na(p01i), 0, p01i), Wind_Speed = sknt ) %>% select(interval60, Temperature, Precipitation, Wind_Speed) %>% distinct(interval60, .keep_all = TRUE) weather_complete <- weather_processed %>% complete(interval60 = seq(min(interval60), max(interval60), by = "hour")) %>% fill(Temperature, Precipitation, Wind_Speed, .direction = "down") # Process weather data weather_processed <- weather_data %>% mutate( interval60 = floor_date(valid, unit = "hour"), Temperature = tmpf, # Temperature in Fahrenheit Precipitation = ifelse(is.na(p01i), 0, p01i), # Hourly precip in inches Wind_Speed = sknt # Wind speed in knots ) %>% select(interval60, Temperature, Precipitation, Wind_Speed) %>% distinct(interval60, .keep_all = TRUE) # Check for missing hours and interpolate if needed weather_complete <- weather_processed %>% complete(interval60 = seq(min(interval60), max(interval60), by = "hour")) %>% fill(Temperature, Precipitation, Wind_Speed, .direction = "down") # Look at the weather summary(weather_complete %>% select(Temperature, Precipitation, Wind_Speed)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Temperature Precipitation Wind_Speed Min. :57.00 Min. :0.0000000 Min. : 0.000 1st Qu.:70.00 1st Qu.:0.0000000 1st Qu.: 4.000 Median :76.00 Median :0.0000000 Median : 6.000 Mean :75.94 Mean :0.0008342 Mean : 6.218 3rd Qu.:81.00 3rd Qu.:0.0000000 3rd Qu.: 8.000 Max. :98.00 Max. :0.1000000 Max. :25.000 ``` ::: ::: ## Visualize Weather Patterns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(weather_complete, aes(x = interval60, y = Temperature)) + geom_line(color = "#3182bd", alpha = 0.7) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "red") + labs( title = "Philadelphia Temperature - Q3 2025", subtitle = "Summer to early fall weather conditions", x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°F)" ) + plotTheme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/visualize-weather-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Temperatures stay pretty high through most of Q3, starting in the upper 70s in July and peaking a bit in early August before gradually cooling into September. Even though there’s a clear downward trend over time, the day-to-day variation is pretty noticeable, with temperatures jumping around quite a bit throughout the quarter. For most of July and August, conditions are consistently warm, which likely supports higher ridership, although the hottest days could also make biking less appealing. By September, temperatures are a bit cooler and probably more comfortable overall, which could help sustain ridership even as summer ends. # CREATE SPACE-TIME PANEL ## Aggregate Trips to Station-Hour Level ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trips_panel <- indego_census %>% group_by( interval60, start_station, start_lat, start_lon, Med_Inc, Percent_Taking_Transit, Percent_White, Total_Pop ) %>% summarize(Trip_Count = n(), .groups = "drop") ``` ::: ## Create Complete Panel Structure Not every station has trips every hour. The distribution is heavily right-skewed, with a long tail of higher values but relatively few instances where trip counts get above 5 or 10. This suggests that while there are occasional periods of higher demand, most station-hours experience very low activity. In other words, high ridership is relatively rare and concentrated in specific times and places rather than being the norm across the system. ## Add Time Features ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} study_panel <- study_panel %>% mutate( week = week(interval60), month = month(interval60, label = TRUE), dotw = wday(interval60, label = TRUE), hour = hour(interval60), date = as.Date(interval60), weekend = ifelse(dotw %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), 1, 0), rush_hour = ifelse(hour %in% c(7, 8, 9, 16, 17, 18), 1, 0) ) ``` ::: ## Join Weather Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} study_panel <- study_panel %>% left_join(weather_complete, by = "interval60") # Check for missing values summary(study_panel %>% select(Trip_Count, Temperature, Precipitation)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Trip_Count Temperature Precipitation Min. : 0.0000 Min. :57.00 Min. :0.0000 1st Qu.: 0.0000 1st Qu.:70.00 1st Qu.:0.0000 Median : 0.0000 Median :76.00 Median :0.0000 Mean : 0.7548 Mean :75.94 Mean :0.0008 3rd Qu.: 1.0000 3rd Qu.:81.00 3rd Qu.:0.0000 Max. :22.0000 Max. :98.00 Max. :0.1000 NA's :6312 NA's :6312 ``` ::: ::: # CREATE TEMPORAL LAG VARIABLES The key innovation for space-time prediction: **past demand predicts future demand**. ## Why Temporal Lags? Temporal lags are especially important in a bikeshare context because demand is often persistent. If a station had high demand one hour ago, it is more likely to have elevated demand now than a station with no recent activity. In other words, temporal dependence helps the model capture short-run demand momentum. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sort by station and time study_panel <- study_panel %>% arrange(start_station, interval60) # Create lag variables WITHIN each station study_panel <- study_panel %>% group_by(start_station) %>% mutate( lag1Hour = lag(Trip_Count, 1), lag2Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 2), lag3Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 3), lag12Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 12), lag1day = lag(Trip_Count, 24) ) %>% ungroup() # Remove rows with NA lags (first 24 hours for each station) study_panel_complete <- study_panel %>% filter(!is.na(lag1day)) ``` ::: ## Visualize Lag Correlations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sample one station to visualize example_station <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(start_station == first(start_station)) %>% head(168) # One week # Plot actual vs lagged demand ggplot(example_station, aes(x = interval60)) + geom_line(aes(y = Trip_Count, color = "Current"), linewidth = 1) + geom_line(aes(y = lag1Hour, color = "1 Hour Ago"), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) + geom_line(aes(y = lag1day, color = "24 Hours Ago"), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) + scale_color_manual(values = c( "Current" = "#08519c", "1 Hour Ago" = "#3182bd", "24 Hours Ago" = "#6baed6" )) + labs( title = "Temporal Lag Patterns at One Station", subtitle = "Past demand predicts future demand", x = "Date-Time", y = "Trip Count", color = "Time Period" ) + plotTheme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/lag_correlations-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # TEMPORAL TRAIN/TEST SPLIT **CRITICAL:** We must train on PAST data and test on FUTURE data! ## Why Temporal Validation Matters In real operations, at the start of September, we would need to predict demand for the rest of the month using only the data available from July and August. We wouldn’t have access to future data because it hasn’t happened yet. Wrong approach: Train the model on later weeks (e.g., late September) and test it on earlier weeks (e.g., July and August). This would mean using future information to predict the past. Correct approach: Train the model on earlier weeks (July through mid/late August) and test it on later weeks (late August through September). This ensures that we are using past data to predict future demand, which better reflects how the model would be used in practice. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Split by week # Q3 has roughly weeks 27-40 (July-Sep) # Train on weeks 27-38 (July through most of September) # Test on weeks 39-40 (late September) # Which stations have trips in BOTH early and late periods? early_stations <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week < 39) %>% filter(Trip_Count > 0) %>% distinct(start_station) %>% pull(start_station) late_stations <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week >= 39) %>% filter(Trip_Count > 0) %>% distinct(start_station) %>% pull(start_station) # Keep only stations that appear in BOTH periods common_stations <- intersect(early_stations, late_stations) # Filter panel to only common stations study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(start_station %in% common_stations) # NOW create train/test split train <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week < 39) test <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week >= 39) # table summary split_summary <- tibble( Dataset = c("Training", "Testing"), Observations = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)), Start_Date = c(min(train$date), min(test$date)), End_Date = c(max(train$date), max(test$date)) ) kable( split_summary %>% mutate(Observations = format(Observations, big.mark = ",")), caption = "Train/Test Split Summary (Q3 2025)" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

On average, the model is off by less than one trip, which may be acceptable for general system planning. However, errors become more problematic during peak demand periods, particularly during the PM rush, when underprediction could lead to empty stations or insufficient bike availability. I would recommend deploying this model as a baseline decision-support tool rather than a fully automated system. It could be useful for identifying general rebalancing patterns and prioritizing high-demand stations, but operators should still rely on real-time monitoring during peak periods when prediction errors are larger and more consequential. There is some evidence that prediction errors vary across neighborhoods, with slightly higher errors in higher-demand, central areas. While these areas may be better served overall, uneven prediction accuracy could still lead to inconsistent service quality. If the model performs worse in certain neighborhoods, it could result in less reliable bike availability, which may disproportionately affect users who rely on bike share for commuting. To avoid reinforcing disparities, safeguards should include monitoring prediction errors across neighborhoods and ensuring minimum service levels regardless of predicted demand. Incorporating equity constraints into rebalancing decisions could help ensure that lower-demand or historically underserved areas are not deprioritized. The model still struggles to capture high-demand spikes, particularly during peak commuting periods and unusual events. This suggests that important drivers of demand, such as special events, real-time weather conditions, and network connectivity, are not fully captured.
